title: Spotting fake login pages
body_md:
## A convincing page can still be the wrong place to sign in

A fake login page borrows a familiar logo, layout and error messages. The attacker needs you to type a password, approve a sign-in, or enter a one-time code into a page they control. Some pages then redirect to the real service so the mistake is less obvious. You cannot judge the recipient of your credentials by the artwork.

### Check the route before the form

Start with how you arrived. An unexpected email, ad, QR code or shared document can send you to a lookalike site. Read the browser's **address bar**, not a domain printed in the page body. A genuine site may use several legitimate domains and external identity providers, so do not invent a universal “exact brand domain” rule. Compare the address and sign-in flow to a bookmark, app or documented route you already use; if unfamiliar, stop and contact the service.

HTTPS encrypts the connection to the site named in the address bar. It does not make that operator honest. A fake page can have HTTPS. The absence of a padlock is a warning for entering secrets, but its presence is not approval.

A password manager may refuse to offer a saved login at a different site, which is a useful pause signal. It may also fail because the form or app changed, the manager is locked, the saved website is wrong, or a legitimate service uses a separate identity provider. Do not override the mismatch by typing a saved password into the page. Return via the known route and ask support if needed. Password managers reduce some phishing risk; they do not make credential theft impossible, especially if users copy passwords or approve prompts elsewhere.

### The moment of entry

Before typing, ask: “Did I intend to reach this service, and does this exact sign-in path match what I know?” If the form asks for extra personal data, a code you did not initiate, or repeated entry after an odd error, stop. These are clues, not a universal fingerprint of fraud. Real services sometimes request step-up verification. Confirm through the account's normal app or support route.

If you already typed a password on a suspect page, leave it, open the real service independently, change that password there, change any reused copies, and review active sessions or contact support. If you approved an MFA request or entered a code, say so when asking the provider or your workplace security team for help. The action depends on what you exposed; no course exercise asks for real credentials.

widget_config.goal: Before entering credentials, verify the actual browser address and sign-in route through a known service path.
widget_config.today_action: Open one account you use from its saved app or bookmark and note the address and normal sign-in handoff, without entering any details into this lesson.
widget_config.scope: General consumer guidance; identity-provider flows vary. Recovery steps depend on the service and workplace policy. Exercises use fictional domains.

blocks.title: Synthetic case: borrowed branding
blocks.situation: A message claiming to be from a file service opens a polished login at https://files-verify.example/sign-in. The page asks for a password and then a one-time code. The browser shows HTTPS.
blocks.analysis: The logo and encryption do not authenticate the operator. The message-origin route and unfamiliar address are enough to stop. Close the tab, open the saved service app, and check for a real notice there. Do not enter a code from an uninitiated sign-in.

blocks.title: Synthetic case: legitimate identity handoff
blocks.situation: At work you open the intranet from your saved bookmark. It redirects to your organization's established identity provider. Your password manager does not suggest a login because it is locked.
blocks.analysis: The missing suggestion alone does not prove phishing. The handoff might be the normal workplace flow. Compare it with the documented sign-in route or ask IT using the directory, then unlock the manager if confirmed. Avoid manually forcing credentials into an uncertain form.

blocks.title: A document that wants a login
blocks.setup: Synthetic exercise. A colleague appears to share a project file; the login page is represented as text only.

steps.prompt: The email button opens a page with a familiar logo and HTTPS. What first?

choices.text: Enter your username; the lock proves the operator.
choices.consequence: You begin disclosing data to an unverified site.
choices.explanation: HTTPS protects transit, not the honesty of the site.

choices.text: Read the browser address and recall your normal file-service route.
choices.consequence: You inspect who will receive the login.
choices.explanation: The browser address and known path matter more than the artwork.

steps.prompt: The address is https://team-files-access.example; your normal app uses another route. What now?

choices.text: Type the password anyway because the file is urgent.
choices.consequence: Credentials may reach the page operator.
choices.explanation: Urgency cannot resolve an unfamiliar sign-in path.

choices.text: Close the page and open the file service through your bookmark.
choices.explanation: The normal route can show whether the file was actually shared.

steps.prompt: When you later check the normal file-service app, no file appears. The alleged colleague is online. How do you verify?

choices.text: Reply to the same email thread.
choices.explanation: Use a separate established channel for the person.

choices.text: Ask the colleague in your existing work chat or in person.
choices.consequence: You test the share claim independently.
choices.explanation: A genuine colleague can confirm without the email path.

steps.prompt: Suppose you already entered a password before pausing. What is the priority?

choices.text: Just close the tab; no loss occurs until a code is entered.
choices.consequence: The password may already be known.
choices.explanation: Do not wait for proof of misuse.

choices.text: Use the real service to change it and tell your security or support team what was entered.
choices.consequence: You start account recovery and preserve a useful incident description.
choices.explanation: Mention any code or approval as well so support can judge exposure.

blocks.debrief: A fake page can be visually exact and encrypted. The reliable move was returning to the known route and, after exposure, responding according to what was entered. Retry each step that let the form set the terms.

questions.prompt: A login page has HTTPS and your bank's logo. What does HTTPS establish?

choices.text: The connection is encrypted to the displayed site, not that the site is the bank.
choices.explanation: The operator may still be fraudulent.
Certificates do not validate a business claim.

questions.prompt: Your manager does not offer a password on a page reached through a message. Best response?

choices.text: Manually type the password to compensate for a possible glitch.
Pause and reach the account through your known route.
choices.explanation: Missing autofill is a clue, not a diagnosis; independent navigation resolves it.

questions.prompt: A bookmarked work site sends you to an unfamiliar identity-provider page. Is that automatically fake?

choices.text: Yes; real sites never redirect for login.
choices.explanation: Legitimate single sign-on can use another domain.

choices.text: No; verify the handoff against your organization's documented flow before entry.
choices.explanation: The unfamiliar route needs confirmation, not an absolute verdict.

questions.prompt: You entered a password on a suspect page but no code. What now?

choices.text: Change it through the real service and seek support; also change reused copies.
choices.explanation: The password could already be exposed.

choices.text: Do nothing because a second factor was not entered.
choices.explanation: An exposed password still requires action.
